In the years after his disastrous coming out, Lewis kept his old neighbourhood—and his mum and dad, Madeleine and David—at a safe distance. But tragedy has been drawing him back: first his parents separated, and now they’ve vanished.

Confronted with the inner lives of his parents—discovered on audio tape recordings and scribbled in journals—their voices feed his imagination as he delves into the mystery of their disappearance.

He’s a writer; he can’t help himself.

Anthony Lapwood (Ngāti Ranginui, Ngāi Te Rangi, Ngāti Whakaue, Pākehā) is a fiction writer based in Te Whanganui-a-Tara Wellington. His writing has appeared in a wide range of publications. Overview

A welcoming men’s circle for honest conversation, deep connection and brotherhood in a space of trust, presence and belonging.

Men’s Circle: Rooted in Connection




Events now start at 6pm. Please try to arrive by 5:45pm so we can get everyone into the event and start on time at 6pm.




The evening offers a supportive space for men to come together, connect, and speak openly about life. Whether you’re moving through a period of change, looking for deeper connection, or simply wanting a space where you can show up as you are, you’re welcome here.

The conversations are honest, open, and grounded in mutual respect. There’s no pressure to speak, share, or have everything figured out. You’re just as welcome to listen and be present. Together, we create a space rooted in confidentiality and non-judgement, where everyone can feel safe, heard, and free to be themselves.

Structure of the Circle
Gathering in a Circle: Participants sit in a circle to symbolize equality and unity.
A short meditation or moment of silence may be included to help everyone arrive and connect.
Talking Object: A sharing stick or object is placed in the center. Only the person holding the object may speak, ensuring uninterrupted sharing.
Open Sharing: Anyone may choose to share while holding the object. Sharing is optional, and passing is always respected.
Active Listening: While one person shares, others listen attentively without speaking, interrupting, or offering advice. The focus is on witnessing and being present.
No Judgments or Advice: Participants refrain from judging or offering unsolicited advice, creating a safe space for authentic expression.
Closing: The circle may conclude with a group reflection, a moment of gratitude, or a simple acknowledgment of the shared experience.
Circle Agreements
Supportive Environment: We are here to uplift and support one another, fostering trust and brotherhood.
Focus on the Present: Share what's alive for you now, focusing on your emotions and experiences to deepen emotional awareness.
Use "I" Statements: Speak from your personal perspective using "I" statements to promote authenticity and responsibility. Avoid generalizations like "we" or "us."
No Judgment or fixing: Refrain from judging others sharing or offering unsolicited advice, ensuring a safe and non-critical space.
Confidentiality: What is shared in the circle stays in the circle. You may discuss your own experience outside the group but keep others' details private.




After the circle, stay for a wholesome plant-based dinner and dessert ($20 or $10 for students). Sharing a meal is a simple way to extend the sense of community and connection. This gathering is offered on a non-profit basis.
Meet Your Host: Sri Jiva

Since childhood, Sri Jiva has been fascinated by meaning, purpose, and authentic life fulfilment. This, among other things, led him to join a monastery at the age of 19. After years of monastic training, he chose to marry and pursue a career. He felt called to use his monastic experience to help others understand themselves, and to find wisdom, meaning, and purpose in their own lives. Inspired by this calling, he went to university to study counselling. Now, Sri Jiva and his wife live near Wellington, where he works with a small team of counsellors, supporting clients individually and in groups.

Ema Frost is a very clever Kiwi Artist, who has been teaching Kintsugi for 5+ years and regularly travels to Japan to study and learn new techniques. Ema's illustrations and ceramic works sit in many of our countries best galleries, and whose products and merchandise sell in the most stylish design stores and gallery shops. Her style is enchanting - quirky, feminine and colourful, and clearly influenced by her travels throughout the world, usually off the beaten track.

Have you ever wanted to try Kintsugi.... It's an ancient Japanese art form where you fix broken pottery with gold - making its imperfections its beauty. - A truly wonderful philosophy to live by. Nothing is ever really broken but new life and meaning is brought back making your piece a work of art and truly something special. You can also apply this technique on various materials like glass, wood, greenstone and shells.

KintsugiIt's called kintsugi (金継ぎ), or kintsukuroi (金繕い), literally golden (“kin”) and repair (“tsugi”). This traditional Japanese art uses a precious metal – liquid gold, liquid silver or lacquer dusted with powdered gold – to bring together the pieces of a broken pottery item and at the same time enhance the breaks.You will take away your wonderful finished work, plus your knew skills which will enable you to further your own Kintsugi in your own time.

A guided kundalini activation. Breath of fire and kundalini pranayama, simple repetitive movement, sound and stillness, sequenced to wake up energy that has been sitting dormant along the spine and let it move.

Who is this for

People who already have some breathwork or movement practice and want something more activating than a wind-down class. You are curious about kundalini but want it held by someone who works with the nervous system, not bypasses it. You are willing to feel a lot and stop when you need to.

Not the right fit as a first-ever breathwork experience. The Root or a gentler breath class is a better start.

What to expect
Arrival and a short orientation: what kundalini activation is, what is normal, and how to opt out of anything
Progressive breath and movement rounds that build energy and heat
A peak where the practice is most active: emotion, shaking, heat, tingling, sound can all come up, all normal
A long, quiet integration: stillness, slow breath, nothing to do
A few minutes to land and share if you want to, before you leave
Benefits
A felt sense of energy moving where it had been stuck
Emotional release without needing a story for it
A reset for a system that has been running flat or wired-and-tired
A clearer, more spacious baseline for a day or two afterward

(No health claims. This is a practice, not a treatment.)

Pre-class prep
Skip heavy food and alcohol in the hours before.
Eat something light beforehand, not a full meal.
Come a few minutes early to settle
If you are pregnant, have a heart or blood-pressure condition, epilepsy, glaucoma, recent surgery, or are in acute mental-health crisis, message Lynn before booking so she can advise or adapt
Wear layers you can move in and get warm in.
Contraindications

Kundalini pranayama and breath of fire are intense. About Lynn

Lynn Tiang is an Integrative Somatic Coach, breathwork facilitator, and Reiki practitioner based in Aotearoa, New Zealand. Lynn supports people who are high-functioning on the outside but chronically tense, exhausted, or quietly stuck on the inside.

Lynn’s work blends three pillars:

Somatic breathwork to regulate the nervous system, soften protective patterns, and restore a steadier baseline in the body
Reiki to support energetic clearing, heart coherence, deep rest, and integration, in a gentle, consent-based way
Life coaching to translate what opens in a session into grounded change in relationships, work, boundaries, and daily life

Lynn’s approach is trauma-aware, practical, and spiritually spacious. The focus isn’t on forcing transformation, it’s on creating enough safety for your system to unwind, receive support, and reconnect with its natural capacity for calm, clarity, and connection.
